Song of Degrees
song of dih-GREEZ
noun
Rendering the Hebrew shīr hammaialōth, “song of the goings-up” or “ascents,” from ‘ālāh, to go up; the title of fifteen psalms sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

A Song of degrees is the title borne by fifteen psalms together, the hundred-and-twentieth through the hundred-and-thirty-fourth. The Hebrew means “songs of the goings-up,” and they are most received as the pilgrim-songs of Israel, sung by the tribes as they went up to Jerusalem — the city set high upon her hills — for the three yearly feasts. Some have tied the “degrees” also to steps, whether the steps of the temple or the going-up of the soul from depth to height; for these psalms do indeed climb. They begin in distress and exile, “In my distress I cried unto the LORD” (Psa 120:1); they lift the eyes to the hills whence cometh help (Psa 121:1); they rejoice at the gates, “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1); and they crown the ascent in the joy of brethren gathered, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psa 133:1). So the Songs of degrees map the upward way of the people of God: from the far country and the lonely tent, step by step, to the courts of the LORD and the communion of the saints. The church is ever a pilgrim church, going up; and these are her marching-songs.

“Songs of the goings-up”; fifteen pilgrim-psalms sung by Israel ascending to Jerusalem for the yearly feasts.

Psa 120, title — "A Song of degrees."

Psa 121:1 — "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Pilgrim-psalms of the going-up; they recover the church’s upward, gathered worship against a privatized and stationary religion.

expand to see more

The Songs of degrees face no postmodern redefinition, but the corporate, ascending worship they embody is much eroded. The age makes religion a private and stationary thing — the lone soul, the solitary screen — with little sense of a people going up together to a holy place to appear before God. The pilgrim-songs rebuke that isolation; they are sung on the road, in company, climbing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church is a pilgrim people, going up together. These psalms move from the far country to the gathered courts, and they crown the ascent not in solitary rapture but in the communion of brethren dwelling in unity. The believer is glad when they say, “Let us go into the house of the LORD”; his worship is a going-up, and he does not go alone.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rendering the Hebrew for “songs of the goings-up,” the Songs of degrees are fifteen pilgrim-psalms of Israel ascending to Jerusalem.

Song of Degrees — Hebrew shīr hammaialōth, “song of the ascents.”

Fifteen psalms bear it, the hundred-and-twentieth through hundred-and-thirty-fourth.

They are the pilgrim-songs sung in going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.

They climb from distress and exile to the joy of the LORD’s courts.

They crown the ascent in the communion of brethren dwelling in unity (Psa 133:1).
